glossary.html: Reconstruction of the full experiment law, including the preparation labels and response records needed to preserve the distinctions available to an experimenter. A convincing fit to a response marginal alone can conceal failures in those joint distinctions. Paper 2 uses statistical comparison to make the reconstruction requirement precise. Read the definitions and results ↗

Whether a declared simulator can reproduce the experiment after a connection is severed, given an explicit resource class. Shared randomness, correlation and communication change the reconstruction problem; declaring those resources is part of the diagnostic. Read the resource comparisons ↗

A representation through which a system's interactions can be modelled while retaining the distinctions required by the declared family of contexts. The relevant object is the complete interaction law, including preparation-response dependence. Read the operational contract ↗

Three separate questions in interface learning: can the representation express an adequate candidate, does the finite-budget learner produce one, and does the calibration rule select it? The matched study separates these events before assessing held-out coverage. Read the diagnostic decomposition ↗

Recovery of binary coordinates from an unlabeled intervention-response family under a declared response model. Paper 4's theorem identifies the chart up to coordinate permutations and independent bit flips under its stated conditions; its approximate results quantify a certification margin. Read the theorem and certificates ↗

A microchart specifies the elementary coordinates used to describe a realization. A macrograin specifies a coarser organization or scale. Identifying a microchart does not itself settle the macrograin: Paper 4 treats the chart-identification theorem and bounded intrinsic-grain comparison as distinct results. Inspect the comparison ↗

faq.question: What do Papers 2–4 add to the monograph?
faq.html: They develop the operational work needed to connect a constitutive account with a physically identified organization. Paper 2 tests and strengthens boundary diagnostics; Paper 3 measures what interface learning actually achieves; Paper 4 identifies binary coordinates under an intervention model and separates that task from selecting a macrograin. The monograph supplies the philosophical and constitutive foundation. Follow the connected research programme ↗

faq.question: Does the new boundary work change the original monograph?
faq.html: The Version 2 monograph is preserved as published. Paper 2 shows that minimal-target masking can alter the candidate graph used by the original construction. It develops stronger reconstruction, resource and composition diagnostics, while distinguishing those diagnostics from a uniquely derived replacement for the phenomenal boundary law. Read the consequences for SPC-2 ↗

faq.question: What does successful interface learning demonstrate?
faq.html: It demonstrates performance against the declared interaction-law criteria, fixtures, contexts and computational budget. Paper 3 reports synthetic experiments, including exact finite comparisons. Its successful learners do not thereby demonstrate consciousness; the phenomenal bridge and realization conditions are additional parts of the framework. The capacity–production–selection decomposition shows where the learning procedure succeeds and where it loses adequate candidates. Read the full learning investigation ↗

faq.question: Does identifying a binary realization also select its grain?
faq.html: No. Paper 4 identifies a microchart under a specified response model and its theorem's assumptions. Macrograin selection remains a separate question. Its executed SPC-2/IIT comparison examines a declared finite search domain; the numerical difference is a result for that domain, not a universal verdict on either framework. Read the identification argument and comparison ↗
